Since the base points are affinely independent, $\det A\ne0$, and the cofactor sign gives $\det A=(-1)^dO_d$.
Expanding the equal power-sphere equations in [A1] gives $h_i-h_0=2c\cdot(p_i-p_0)$ for $1\le i\le d$. For the query row, the same expansion gives $h_q-h_0=2c\cdot(q-p_0)+\Delta(q)$.

In the lifted determinant defining $P_d$, subtract row $p_0$ from all other rows and expand along the final column. The cofactor sign is $(-1)^{d+3}$. Subtract $2c_j$ times coordinate column $j$ from the lifted-height column for every $j$; by [step 1.2] the first $d$ height entries become zero and the query height entry becomes $\Delta(q)$. derivations.claim: Choose three distinct sites $p_1,p_2,p_3$ whose cells contain $x$. From $x\in V(p_i)$, $\|x-p_i\|^2\le\|x-p_j\|^2$ for every $j$; reversing $i,j$ gives equality. Thus all sites whose cells contain $x$ have the same squared distance $r^2$ from $x$. For every other site $q$, the defining inequality gives $r^2\le\|x-q\|^2$, so none is strictly inside the circle.

The common radius is positive, since radius zero would force every site whose cell contains $x$ to equal $x$, contradicting distinctness and the existence of three sites. A line intersects the circle $\|y-x\|^2=r^2$ in at most two points: parameterizing the line as $y=a+tv$ gives a nonzero quadratic equation in $t$. Hence no three of the sites on the circle are collinear. For any one such site $p$, the tangent line at $p$ supports the disk and meets the circle only at $p$; therefore $p$ cannot be a convex combination of the other circle sites. All nearest sites are extreme points of their convex hull, so that hull is a polygon with these sites as its vertices.

derivations.claim: Expand the determinant polynomial in [F3] along its lifted-height column. It has constant coefficient equal to the original determinant and one perturbation term for each row; the coefficient of the query row's perturbation is its cofactor, which is $O_d$ up to sign. By [A1] this coefficient is nonzero, so the polynomial is not identically zero.

The exponents $2^{r_i}$ are distinct because the ranks in [F3] are distinct across the fixed universe [F1]. Thus no two perturbation terms have the same exponent and their nonzero coefficients cannot cancel. The sign selected by the procedure is exactly the sign of the first nonzero coefficient in this one polynomial, so it is a well-defined sign of one common lifted tuple, not a separate choice for each predicate.

If the original determinant is nonzero, its constant coefficient is the unique term of exponent $0$, while all perturbation exponents are positive; therefore the first nonzero coefficient is the original determinant and its sign is unchanged. If the original determinant is zero, step 1.1 shows a nonzero tie polynomial and step 2.1 gives its unique first coefficient. The finite set $U$ supplies one fixed rank assignment for every tuple, so the signs are coherent and the procedure uses no arbitrary epsilon choice.

Throughout this page, $\mathbb R$ is a commutative field with $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and the least-upper-bound property. Let $\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its dyadic subfield. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, a nonempty finite indexed site list is a finite list
$$S=((\iota_1,p_1,w_1),\ldots,(\iota_N,p_N,w_N)),$$
where every $\iota_i\in\mathbb Z$ is a distinct stable identifier, every $p_i\in\mathbb D^d$, and each optional weight $w_i$ is either absent (meaning $0$) or belongs to $\mathbb D$. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

For a finite point set $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $P$. Its affine dimension is the dimension of its affine hull. A tuple $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is affinely independent when the vectors $p_1-p_0,\ldots,p_d-p_0$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^d$; here a basis means every vector has a unique linear expansion in those vectors. This convention makes nondegenerate simplex coordinates unique.

Take a fixed finite universe $U$ of indexed sites as in [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]], dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$, and an ordered tuple of $d+2$ sites from $U$ with distinct identifiers. A computation using auxiliary sites, such as a planar supertriangle, includes those sites in $U$ from the start and assigns them distinct deterministic integer identifiers. Require that the first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent. Put $h_i=\|p_i\|^2-w_i$, with absent weights interpreted as $0$. Rank all identifiers of $U$ in increasing order, starting at rank $0$, and define
$$P(\varepsilon)=\det\bigl((p_i,h_i+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}},1)\bigr)_{i=0}^{d+1}.$$
Regard $\varepsilon$ as a positive formal infinitesimal in the rational-function field $\mathbb R(\varepsilon)$, ordered so a nonzero polynomial has the sign of its coefficient at its least nonzero exponent. Expand this finite polynomial exactly and return the sign of its coefficient at the least exponent with nonzero coefficient. If the base is degenerate, return status degenerate-base. The same universe $U$ and ranks are used for every predicate tuple. The procedure never chooses or evaluates a numerical $\varepsilon$; its returned sign is the declared stable-id tie convention for the raw lifted determinant in [[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]].

Fix one finite universe $U$ of uniquely indexed dyadic sites and weights and a dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. For an ordered tuple of $d+2$ distinct sites whose first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent, the lexicographic lift procedure in [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]] is the determinant sign of one common formal lifted configuration. Every exact nonzero power determinant retains its original sign, every exact zero has a nonzero polynomial tie determinant, and all tuples therefore receive mutually coherent signs. No numeric perturbation parameter is selected or assumed.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $p_0,\ldots,p_d,q\in\mathbb D^d$, and let their dyadic weights be $w_0,\ldots,w_d,w_q$ (zero when absent). Assume $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ are affinely independent. If $c\in\mathbb R^d$ and $R\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$$\|p_i-c\|^2-w_i=R\qquad(0\le i\le d),$$
define the power difference
$$\Delta(q)=\|q-c\|^2-w_q-R.$$
Let $O_d$ be the determinant of the rows $(p_i,1)$ for $i=0,\ldots,d$, and let $P_d$ be the determinant of the $d+2$ rows $(p_i,\|p_i\|^2-w_i,1)$, including the query row $(q,\|q\|^2-w_q,1)$. Then
$$P_d=-O_d\Delta(q),\qquad O_dP_d=-O_d^2\Delta(q).$$
Thus the sign of $O_dP_d$ is positive, zero or negative exactly when $q$ is respectively inside, on or outside the power sphere. When all weights are zero, this is the ordinary circumsphere convention.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}(P)$. A feasible representation is a vector $(\lambda_i)_{i\in P}$ with $\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$, and $\sum_i\lambda_i p_i=x$. Its formal height is $H(\lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i h_i$. If its support has more than $d+1$ sites, the vectors $(p_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ are linearly dependent, so there is a nonzero vector $(\alpha_i)$ on that support with $\sum_i\alpha_i=0$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i p_i=0$. Such a vector has both positive and negative entries. Choose one of the two directions $\lambda+t\alpha$ that does not increase $H$ and increase $|t|$ until a coefficient first becomes zero. This preserves feasibility and reduces support. Repeating finitely gives a feasible representation of support at most $d+1$ with no greater height.

There are finitely many supports of size at most $d+1$. For any affinely independent support, its coefficients representing $x$ are unique; any dependent support reduces by step 1.1. Therefore the minimum formal height among feasible representations is attained among a finite nonempty set of basic supports.

Exclude temporarily the finite union of convex hulls of subsets of at most $d$ sites. For an $x$ outside this union, choose a minimizing support of smallest cardinality; it has exactly $d+1$ sites, is affinely independent, and has strictly positive coefficients $\lambda_i$. Indeed, a dependent support reduces by step 1.1 without increasing its minimal height, contradicting minimal cardinality. For any other site $q$, write its unique affine coordinates $q=\sum_i\alpha_i p_i$, $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, replacing $\lambda_i$ by $\lambda_i-t\alpha_i$ and adding coefficient $t$ at $q$ remains feasible. Minimality gives $h_q-\sum_i\alpha_i h_i\ge0$. Hence the hyperplane through the lifted support sites lies below every lifted site and its projected simplex contains $x$.

The set excluded in step 3.1 lies in a finite union of proper affine subspaces. A line segment in any open ball of $\operatorname{int}\operatorname{conv}(P)$ can be chosen in a direction not parallel to any of these subspaces; each subspace then removes at most one point of the segment. Thus the complement is dense in the interior. The interior is dense in the whole convex hull: join any hull point to a fixed interior point, and every point of the joining segment other than the hull endpoint is interior by convexity. There are finitely many $d$-tuples of sites, hence finitely many lower simplices; their projected simplices are closed. Step 3.1 puts a dense subset of $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ in their union, so that finite union covers the entire convex hull.

If a lower hyperplane contained at least $d+2$ lifted sites, its projected face would contain a nondegenerate $d$-tuple and an additional site, contradicting the nonzero determinant from [F3]. Thus every full-dimensional lower cell is a simplex. If two projected lower simplices have support planes $L_1,L_2$, all their vertices lie on or above both supporting planes. For a point $x$ in the intersection of their projections, the two lifted convex combinations at $x$ therefore force $L_1(x)\ge L_2(x)$ and $L_2(x)\ge L_1(x)$; hence $L_1(x)=L_2(x)$. On each simplex the corresponding plane difference has one sign at every vertex, so its zero set is a face. If $L_1=L_2$, the nonzero determinant [F3] forces the same $d+1$ vertices. Thus intersections are common faces.

The supporting inequality for a formal lift has nonnegative constant-term difference at each site; otherwise its negative constant coefficient would force a negative formal sign by [F3]. The constant terms therefore give the unperturbed weak support inequalities, and [F4] identifies them with empty power spheres.

e v}\mu_ux_u$. Thus $Q_v=\operatorname{conv}\{x_u:u
e v\}$. The cone is four-dimensional because the vertex differences span $\mathbb R^4$, so its transverse section is three-dimensional. A face of this cone is generated by the directions of the corresponding face of $Q$ through $v$: a supporting linear inequality of the cone restricts to a supporting inequality of $Q$ tight at $v$, and conversely the facets active at $v$ define the cone. Therefore its extreme rays correspond to edges at $v$, and its three-dimensional faces correspond to facets of $Q$ containing $v$. A facet of $Q$ not containing $v$ misses the section because all its vertices lie below the section level. Intersecting cone faces with the transverse section lowers dimension by one, so the vertices of $Q_v$ correspond to edges of $Q$ at $v$ and its facets correspond to facets of $Q$ containing $v$. Write $d_v,t_v$ for the numbers of vertices and facets of $Q_v$.

Choose a facet $F_0$ of $Q_v$. A viewpoint just outside a relative-interior point of $F_0$ gives a Schlegel projection onto its plane: each ray through an interior point of $F_0$ enters $Q_v$ there and, by convexity and boundedness, has a unique exit point on the opposite boundary. The set of such viewpoints contains an open region. The exit points cover $F_0$; uniqueness makes projected facet interiors disjoint, and shared edges project to shared boundaries. Choose the viewpoint generically within this region so projected vertices are distinct and no three projected vertices are collinear. Let $T$ be a nondegenerate triangle with ordered vertices $p_0,p_1,p_2\in\mathbb D^2$. For $x\in\mathbb R^2$, its **barycentric coordinates** are the unique scalars $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ satisfying $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$ and $x=\sum_i\lambda_i p_i$. They are exact for dyadic $x$: they are obtained by solving the invertible $2\times2$ system with columns $p_1-p_0,p_2-p_0$. The point is in $T$ exactly when all $\lambda_i\ge0$.

Given vertex data $f_0,f_1,f_2\in\mathbb R$, the **barycentric affine interpolant** on $T$ is $I_Tf(x)=\sum_i\lambda_i f_i$. A point-location result is a containing triangle of the triangulation, with a shared-edge or shared-vertex result allowed when the point lies on a face; outside the convex hull its status is `outside-hull` and no containing triangle is returned.

For a finite unweighted site set $P$, the **nearest-site query** returns a site minimizing $\|x-p\|^2$, breaking ties by the least stable identifier. Its hull status is `inside-hull` for $x\in\operatorname{conv}P$ and `outside-hull` otherwise. The minimizer is returned in either case.

Use the unweighted deduplicated coordinate set of [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]. If its affine dimension is zero, its output is its single site. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

For affine dimension two, a **triangulation of the sites** is a finite family of nondegenerate closed triangles whose vertices are sites, whose union is the convex hull, and whose pairwise intersections are common faces. Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. The boundary edges of the convex hull are subdivided at every site on that boundary. A triangle is **weakly empty-circle** when no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk; other sites may lie on its boundary.

For each site $p$, its closed **Voronoi cell** is
$$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$
A tie belongs to every minimizing cell. The **Delaunay graph** has one vertex for each site and an edge $pq$ exactly when $V(p)\cap V(q)$ contains a nontrivial line segment. A **Voronoi vertex** is a point belonging to at least three distinct cells. It is dual to the convex polygon of the nearest sites; [[lem-voronoi-vertex-empty-circle]] proves that those sites are vertices on one empty circle centered at that point. A **Delaunay triangulation** is a triangulation refining these polygonal Delaunay faces and having weakly empty circumdisks. In a cocircular face the triangulation need not be unique; the chosen algorithmic refinement is the fixed-universe convention of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

The convex-hull boundary is the boundary of the union of the triangles. An unbounded Voronoi cell corresponds to a site on that boundary. No minimum-angle or other mesh-quality condition is part of these definitions.

Let $F$ be a field, let $a,b\in F$ with $a\ne b$, and let $y_0,y_1\in F$. The unique polynomial $P\in F[X]$ of degree at most one with $P(a)=y_0$ and $P(b)=y_1$ is
$$P(X)=y_0+(y_1-y_0)\frac{X-a}{b-a}.$$

Assume a finite full-dimensional planar site set in general position: no three input sites are collinear and no four are cocircular. Choose the augmented dyadic supertriangle by calling `CHOOSE-SUPERTRIANGLE(P,1)` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], so the full augmented set has no three collinear sites and no four cocircular sites. Fix the common tie ranks before processing.

Draw one permutation uniformly from all $n!$ permutations of the distinct input sites. Initialize the fixed-universe supertriangle and current triangulation as in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], and maintain a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose leaves correspond one-to-one with current triangulation triangles. Initially the DAG has one leaf for the supertriangle.

For each next site $p$, start at the root. At each node, order its child triangles lexicographically by their sorted vertex identifiers and test each child by the same three signed-orientation containment tests used by `INSERT` in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. Descend to the unique child containing $p$ until reaching a current leaf $T$. Under the augmented general-position condition, $p$ lies in the interior of a unique triangle at every stage; the located leaf therefore supplies the face certificate `face(T)`. Call `INSERT(p,face(T))` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. The update verifies that certificate, uses it without a triangle scan, and returns the ordered replacement events. Process those events in order: for a face split, replace the old leaf by pointers to its three new triangle leaves; for an interior-edge split, replace each of the two old leaves by pointers to the two new triangles whose interiors meet that old triangle; for a flip, point each of the two old leaves to both new triangle leaves. Each event names the triangles and overlap map as specified by the insertion procedure. A leaf replaced later is treated in the same way, so the graph remains acyclic and its current leaves correspond exactly to the current triangulation. The insertion procedure also accepts an interior-edge certificate from callers whose admissible inputs permit edge hits; this randomized variant's general-position condition excludes that case. Each internal node has at most three children. After construction, remove synthetic-vertex triangles for the returned Delaunay triangulation; the history DAG is the insertion-time point-location structure.

For every nonempty finite indexed dyadic planar site set, after duplicate collapse the algorithm of [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]] terminates. In the affine-dimension-two branch, after each insertion the augmented triangles are exactly the $d=2$ lower simplices of the common fixed-universe formal lift, as defined in [[lem-lower-lifted-facets-cover-the-convex-hull]]. After removing synthetic vertices, the output triangulates the input convex hull with weakly empty original circumdisks and coherent lexicographic ties. In dimensions zero and one, the algorithm returns the defined single site or consecutive chain.

For a triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites with affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $T$ the number of triangles, and $E$ the number of edges. Then
$$T=2n-2-k,\qquad E=3n-3-k.$$
In particular $T<2n$ and $E<3n$.

Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $p_0,\ldots,p_d,q\in\mathbb D^d$, and let their dyadic weights be $w_0,\ldots,w_d,w_q$ (zero when absent). Assume $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ are affinely independent. If $c\in\mathbb R^d$ and $R\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$$\|p_i-c\|^2-w_i=R\qquad(0\le i\le d),$$
define the power difference
$$\Delta(q)=\|q-c\|^2-w_q-R.$$
Let $O_d$ be the determinant of the rows $(p_i,1)$ for $i=0,\ldots,d$, and let $P_d$ be the determinant of the $d+2$ rows $(p_i,\|p_i\|^2-w_i,1)$, including the query row $(q,\|q\|^2-w_q,1)$. Then
$$P_d=-O_d\Delta(q),\qquad O_dP_d=-O_d^2\Delta(q).$$
Thus the sign of $O_dP_d$ is positive, zero or negative exactly when $q$ is respectively inside, on or outside the power sphere. When all weights are zero, this is the ordinary circumsphere convention.

derivations.claim: Let $S_r$ be the unordered set of the first $r$ input sites, and let $p_r$ be the last site among them. Conditional on $S_r$, $p_r$ is uniform on $S_r$. The augmented triangulation has $m=r+3$ vertices and its fixed hull has $k=3$ sites, so [F3] gives $T_r=2r+1$ and $E_r=3r+3$. The conditional expected degree of uniform $p_r$ equals the average input-site degree, hence is at most $(2E_r)/r=6+6/r\le12$. The number of final triangles incident to $p_r$ is its degree. During local legalization, the initial face split creates three triangles and each flip adds two triangles while increasing that degree by one; if the final degree is $d_r$, at most $2d_r-3$ triangle nodes are created in that stage. Thus expected DAG nodes per stage are at most $21$, and the DAG has expected $O(n)$ nodes.

Fix a stage $r$ and condition on $S_r$. Let $k_r(q)$ count the triangles of its Delaunay triangulation whose circumdisks contain a future site $q$, and let $k_r(q,p_r)$ count those also incident to $p_r$. Since the triangulation $T_r$ is determined by the unordered set $S_r$, it is fixed under this conditioning. Each triangle has at most three input vertices, so uniformity of $p_r$ gives $\mathbb E[k_r(q,p_r)\mid S_r]\le3k_r(q)/r$. The new final triangles are exactly those of $T_r$ incident to $p_r$, and therefore $\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{\Delta\in T_r\setminus T_{r-1}}|K(\Delta)|\,\middle|\,S_r\right]=\sum_{q\notin S_r}\mathbb E[k_r(q,p_r)\mid S_r]\le\frac3r\sum_{q\notin S_r}k_r(q)$.

Count first the triangles in the final Delaunay triangulations $T_r$ that are created at a stage; for such a triangle $\Gamma$, let $K(\Gamma)$ be the set of later input sites strictly inside its circumdisk. A DAG walk visits only triangle nodes containing its query: a split's children partition the replaced triangle, and a flip's two linked children together cover each of the two replaced triangles. If a visited node is destroyed by a face split, it is the old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ being split; the query lies inside it and hence in $K(\Gamma)$. If it is destroyed by a flip, the flip removes an old Delaunay triangle $\Gamma$ whose circumdisk contains the inserted site, together with one triangle incident to that site. The latter triangle lies in the same disk because its vertices are in the disk and the disk is convex. Charge either visited node to $\Gamma$. Each old $\Gamma$ is deleted once and is paired with at most one inserted-site triangle, so it receives at most two charges per query. Consequently the total number of visits is $O(n+\sum_{\Gamma}|K(\Gamma)|)$.

Conditional on $S_r$, the next site $q=p_{r+1}$ is uniform among the $n-r$ remaining sites, so $\sum_{q\notin S_r}k_r(q)=(n-r)\mathbb E[k_r(p_{r+1})\mid S_r]$. Every old triangle's plane supports all sites in $S_r$ by [F2]. By [F4], a future site is strictly inside its circumcircle exactly when its lifted point is formally below this plane; augmented general position excludes equality. Thus precisely the triangles counted by $k_r(p_{r+1})$ cease to support after the insertion, and [F2] returns the new lower triangulation, so this count is exactly the number of old triangles destroyed. The hull remains the same supertriangle, so [F3] gives $T_{r+1}-T_r=2$; the number destroyed is the number of final triangles created minus $2$, hence at most that number. After averaging over $S_r$, the set $S_{r+1}$ is a uniform $(r+1)$-subset and $p_{r+1}$ is uniform within it; step 1.1 bounds the expected number of final triangles created by $12$. Thus $\mathbb E[k_r(p_{r+1})]\le12$, and averaging step 1.2 gives a stage-$r$ expected conflict sum at most $36(n-r)/r$.

Summing the bound of step 2.2 over $r=1,\ldots,n-1$ gives at most $36n\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}1/r=O(n\log n)$. Step 2.1 then bounds expected DAG traversal work by $O(n\log n)$. The located face is passed to `INSERT` and verified with at most four exact orientation calls per insertion; the update does not run the triangle scan, so this adds only $O(n)$ predicate calls. Triangle updates and storage are expected $O(n)$.

At stage $r$ the augmented triangulation has $r+3$ vertices, so the inserted site's degree is at most $r+2$. By step 1.1, which counts at most $2d_r-3$ new triangle nodes when the final degree is $d_r$, each stage creates $O(r)$ nodes and the whole DAG has $O(n^2)$ nodes. Each of $n$ queries visits at most all those nodes, with at most three child tests per node by [F1]. Thus worst-case total location work is $O(n^3)$. The count is in exact predicate calls; arbitrary-precision bit cost is not included.

For a weighted site $(p,w)$, define its power distance from $x\in\mathbb R^3$ by
$$\pi_{(p,w)}(x)=\|x-p\|^2-w.$$
Its lifted point is $\widehat p=(p,\|p\|^2-w)\in\mathbb R^4$. A lower face of the lifted convex hull is a face supported by a nonvertical hyperplane $z=\ell(x)$ with every lifted site on or above that hyperplane. The projection of the union of lower faces is the **regular subdivision** of the projected sites; a simplex in that subdivision has an empty power sphere, meaning its common power distance is no larger than that of any input site.

The lex-refined lift is interpreted over the ordered rational-function field of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]], using one fixed finite universe of all input sites. When every weight is zero, the regular subdivision is the ordinary 3D Delaunay subdivision and power spheres are circumspheres. A weight configuration can hide a site: a weighted site is **hidden** if its lift is not a vertex of any lower face. A nonsimplicial lower face is refined with the same fixed-universe lexicographic lift convention. For projected affine dimension below three, the algorithm reports `lower-dimensional` with that dimension and the exact deduplicated site list, and makes no tetrahedralization claim. A tetrahedral output is claimed only on the full-dimensional branch with nondegenerate projected bases.

Fix one finite universe $U$ of uniquely indexed dyadic sites and weights and a dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. For an ordered tuple of $d+2$ distinct sites whose first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent, the lexicographic lift procedure in [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]] is the determinant sign of one common formal lifted configuration. Every exact nonzero power determinant retains its original sign, every exact zero has a nonzero polynomial tie determinant, and all tuples therefore receive mutually coherent signs. Let $Q$ be a full-dimensional convex polytope in $\mathbb R^4$ with $m\ge5$ vertices. A facet is a three-dimensional face, and a vertex is an extreme point. Then the number $f_3$ of facets satisfies
$$f_3\le \frac{m(m-3)}2.$$

For a finite dyadic weighted site set of projected affine dimension three, the algorithm of [[alg-incremental-three-dimensional-regular-cavity-repair]] terminates. Its output tetrahedra cover the convex hull, meet in common faces, and have empty power spheres in the original weak sense. In the zero-weight case they are ordinary Delaunay tetrahedra. derivations.claim: Assume $n\ge5$. For each five-site tuple whose projected points contain four affinely independent sites, order four such sites first and the fifth last, and let $P(\varepsilon)$ be its lifted determinant polynomial. By [F2], this polynomial is nonzero. Write it as $c\varepsilon^k+\sum_j c_j\varepsilon^{k_j}$, where $c\ne0$ and every $k_j>k$. If $C=\sum_j|c_j|>0$, then for $0<\varepsilon<\min(1,|c|/(2C))$, the absolute value of the higher terms after dividing by $\varepsilon^k$ is at most $C\varepsilon<|c|/2$, since each $k_j-k$ is a positive integer; if $C=0$, its sign is constant for every $\varepsilon>0$. Thus each such determinant has its formal sign for all sufficiently small positive real $\varepsilon$. There are finitely many relevant tuples, so choose one positive real $\varepsilon$ small enough for all of them. Use this same value to evaluate the heights of every site. By [F4], each output tetrahedron is a lower simplex of the formal lift. On its affinely independent projected base, every other site's formal support determinant is nonzero by [F2]; the preceding sign specialization preserves its sign. If $O$ is the projected orientation determinant of the base, $h_q$ is the query height, and $\ell(q)$ is the height of the base graph plane at the query, row subtraction gives the displayed-order identity $P=-O(h_q-\ell(q))$. As $O\ne0$ and is unchanged by height specialization, the same four real lifted points support a real lower facet and every other lifted point lies strictly above it. No fifth point is in that facet. Distinct output tetrahedra therefore correspond to distinct facets of this one real convex hull.

If $n=4$, at most one four-site candidate is output, and $1\le4(4-3)/2$. If $n\ge5$, choose four affinely independent projected sites and a fifth distinct site. Their formal determinant is nonzero by [F2], and its real specialization at the common value from step 1.1 is nonzero. Hence the real lifted convex hull is full-dimensional in $\mathbb R^4$. Let $m\le n$ be its number of extreme vertices; full dimension forces $m\ge5$.

Apply [F3] to this full-dimensional convex 4-polytope. Its total number of facets, hence also its number of lower facets, is at most $m(m-3)/2$. By step 1.1, the output tetrahedra inject into those facets. The function $s(s-3)/2$ is increasing for integers $s\ge5$, so the output count is at most $n(n-3)/2$. This is quadratic; the argument establishes no angle or tetrahedral-quality bound.

Throughout this page, $\mathbb R$ is a commutative field with $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and the least-upper-bound property. Let $\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its dyadic subfield. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, a nonempty finite indexed site list is a finite list
$$S=((\iota_1,p_1,w_1),\ldots,(\iota_N,p_N,w_N)),$$
where every $\iota_i\in\mathbb Z$ is a distinct stable identifier, every $p_i\in\mathbb D^d$, and each optional weight $w_i$ is either absent (meaning $0$) or belongs to $\mathbb D$. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

For a finite point set $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $P$. Its affine dimension is the dimension of its affine hull. A tuple $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is affinely independent when the vectors $p_1-p_0,\ldots,p_d-p_0$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^d$; here a basis means every vector has a unique linear expansion in those vectors. This convention makes nondegenerate simplex coordinates unique.

Take a fixed finite universe $U$ of indexed sites as in [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]], dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$, and an ordered tuple of $d+2$ sites from $U$ with distinct identifiers. A computation using auxiliary sites, such as a planar supertriangle, includes those sites in $U$ from the start and assigns them distinct deterministic integer identifiers. Require that the first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent. Put $h_i=\|p_i\|^2-w_i$, with absent weights interpreted as $0$. Rank all identifiers of $U$ in increasing order, starting at rank $0$, and define
$$P(\varepsilon)=\det\bigl((p_i,h_i+\varepsilon^{2^{r_i}},1)\bigr)_{i=0}^{d+1}.$$
Regard $\varepsilon$ as a positive formal infinitesimal in the rational-function field $\mathbb R(\varepsilon)$, ordered so a nonzero polynomial has the sign of its coefficient at its least nonzero exponent. Expand this finite polynomial exactly and return the sign of its coefficient at the least exponent with nonzero coefficient. If the base is degenerate, return status degenerate-base. The same universe $U$ and ranks are used for every predicate tuple. The procedure never chooses or evaluates a numerical $\varepsilon$; its returned sign is the declared stable-id tie convention for the raw lifted determinant in [[def-certified-geometric-predicate-determinants]].

No numeric perturbation parameter is selected or assumed.

Use the unweighted deduplicated coordinate set of [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]. If its affine dimension is zero, its output is its single site. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

For affine dimension two, a **triangulation of the sites** is a finite family of nondegenerate closed triangles whose vertices are sites, whose union is the convex hull, and whose pairwise intersections are common faces. Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. The boundary edges of the convex hull are subdivided at every site on that boundary. A triangle is **weakly empty-circle** when no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk; other sites may lie on its boundary.

For each site $p$, its closed **Voronoi cell** is
$$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$
A tie belongs to every minimizing cell. The **Delaunay graph** has one vertex for each site and an edge $pq$ exactly when $V(p)\cap V(q)$ contains a nontrivial line segment. A **Voronoi vertex** is a point belonging to at least three distinct cells. It is dual to the convex polygon of the nearest sites; [[lem-voronoi-vertex-empty-circle]] proves that those sites are vertices on one empty circle centered at that point. A **Delaunay triangulation** is a triangulation refining these polygonal Delaunay faces and having weakly empty circumdisks. In a cocircular face the triangulation need not be unique; the chosen algorithmic refinement is the fixed-universe convention of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

The convex-hull boundary is the boundary of the union of the triangles. An unbounded Voronoi cell corresponds to a site on that boundary. No minimum-angle or other mesh-quality condition is part of these definitions.

Throughout this page, $\mathbb R$ is a commutative field with $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and the least-upper-bound property. Let $\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$ be its dyadic subfield. For $d\in\{2,3\}$, a nonempty finite indexed site list is a finite list
$$S=((\iota_1,p_1,w_1),\ldots,(\iota_N,p_N,w_N)),$$
where every $\iota_i\in\mathbb Z$ is a distinct stable identifier, every $p_i\in\mathbb D^d$, and each optional weight $w_i$ is either absent (meaning $0$) or belongs to $\mathbb D$. In unweighted mode, a duplicate means equal coordinates; collapse each such class to its least identifier. In weighted mode, a duplicate means an equal coordinate-weight pair; collapse only equal pairs to the least identifier. Equal coordinates with unequal weights remain distinct weighted sites.

The unweighted deduplicated set keeps, for each coordinate value $p$, the entry with least identifier among entries at $p$, and records each discarded identifier in a duplicate map. The weighted deduplicated set keeps the least identifier for each exact pair $(p,w)$ and records only repeated pairs in its duplicate map. A weighted computation retains different weights at the same coordinate; their power values are compared by the ordinary power-distance rule, so a dominated weight may be hidden.

For a finite point set $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of points of $P$. Its affine dimension is the dimension of its affine hull. A tuple $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is affinely independent when the vectors $p_1-p_0,\ldots,p_d-p_0$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^d$; here a basis means every vector has a unique linear expansion in those vectors. This convention makes nondegenerate simplex coordinates unique.

Use the unweighted deduplicated coordinate set of [[def-indexed-geometric-site-set]]. If its affine dimension is zero, its output is its single site. If its affine dimension is one, sort by the first varying coordinate (use $x$ if it varies, otherwise $y$) and take the chain joining consecutive sites; this is the lower-dimensional output and contains no triangles.

For affine dimension two, a **triangulation of the sites** is a finite family of nondegenerate closed triangles whose vertices are sites, whose union is the convex hull, and whose pairwise intersections are common faces. Its 1-skeleton is the graph with these sites as vertices and all triangle sides as edges; it is connected. The bounded faces of this plane graph are exactly the chosen triangles, and its one unbounded face is the exterior of the convex hull. The boundary edges of the convex hull are subdivided at every site on that boundary. A triangle is **weakly empty-circle** when no site lies strictly inside its circumdisk; other sites may lie on its boundary.

For each site $p$, its closed **Voronoi cell** is
$$V(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x-p\|^2\le\|x-q\|^2\text{ for every site }q\}.$$
A tie belongs to every minimizing cell. The **Delaunay graph** has one vertex for each site and an edge $pq$ exactly when $V(p)\cap V(q)$ contains a nontrivial line segment. A **Voronoi vertex** is a point belonging to at least three distinct cells. It is dual to the convex polygon of the nearest sites; [[lem-voronoi-vertex-empty-circle]] proves that those sites are vertices on one empty circle centered at that point. A **Delaunay triangulation** is a triangulation refining these polygonal Delaunay faces and having weakly empty circumdisks. In a cocircular face the triangulation need not be unique; the chosen algorithmic refinement is the fixed-universe convention of [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]].

The convex-hull boundary is the boundary of the union of the triangles. An unbounded Voronoi cell corresponds to a site on that boundary. No minimum-angle or other mesh-quality condition is part of these definitions.

For every nonempty finite indexed dyadic planar site set, after duplicate collapse the algorithm of [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]] terminates. In the affine-dimension-two branch, after each insertion the augmented triangles are exactly the $d=2$ lower simplices of the common fixed-universe formal lift, as defined in [[lem-lower-lifted-facets-cover-the-convex-hull]]. After removing synthetic vertices, the output triangulates the input convex hull with weakly empty original circumdisks and coherent lexicographic ties. In dimensions zero and one, the algorithm returns the defined single site or consecutive chain.

For a triangulation of the convex hull of $n$ distinct planar sites with affine dimension two, let $k$ be the number of sites on the hull boundary, $T$ the number of triangles, and $E$ the number of edges. Then
$$T=2n-2-k,\qquad E=3n-3-k.$$
In particular $T<2n$ and $E<3n$.
